paper_title: DeFT-RAG: Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) now perform strongly across a wide
range of language tasks [19, 28]. Yet because their knowledge is
stored in their parameters, they often answer incorrectly when that
knowledge is outdated or missing, and they may hallucinate [11].
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [5, 15] mitigates this by
retrieving passages from an external corpus and grounding the
sections.content: answer in them, which improves accuracy on knowledge-intensive tasks without retraining the model. single retrieve-then-generate step suffices when one passage holds the answer, but it falls short on multi-hop question answering [9, 24, 29], where answering one question requires chaining several facts spread across different documents: retrieving with the question alone returns passages that match its surface terms, and these rarely cover every link of the chain. Graph-based RAG methods [2, 4, 68, 27] address this by building graph over the corpus that links entities and passages, then retrieving passages by following links from the entities in the question. However, multi-hop chain runs through bridge entities that the question never names and that only become known once an earlier step is answered. Because most graph-based methods retrieve once per question, starting from the entities the question names, they can reach the bridge entities only by following graph links from those entities, which rarely gets past the first one: for most of these methods, the full evidence chain is retrieved for only 610% of 3-hop MuSiQue questions (Figure 1a, Table 3). Iterative RAG methods [3, 14, 20, 25] instead aim to find these bridge entities directly: they decompose the question into subquestions and alternate between retrieval and LLM reasoning, so each answered sub-question supplies the bridge entity needed by the next retrieval. However, their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, often within one call, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding the dependencies among them, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known, each of which leads to its own type of error. Specifically, plan written before any sub-question is answered must guess bridge entities, and wrong guess or missing step misleads every later step (planning errors). The dependencies decided among the subquestions may link them wrongly or in the wrong order, so subquestion is searched before the fact it needs is found (dependency errors), as in Figure 1b. When an answer arrives, the LLM may fail to rewrite the sub-question that depends on it, which keeps placeholder instead of the entitys name, or may rewrite it with the wrong entity (rewriting errors). In long, growing input, the LLM may also lose track of what it has already found (tracking errors), as in Figure 1c. Moreover, fixed top-𝑘 retrieval, used by most RAG methods, makes these issues worse by lowering the answer accuracy at each step. Finally, iterative methods discard their intermediate results once question is answered, although multi-hop questions over the same corpus often share intermediate facts that could be reused. Based on these observations, we propose DeFT-RAG, RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at time from the original question Dingyi Kang and Bingzhe Li Figure 1: Failures of graph-based and iterative RAG on 3-hop MuSiQue question (gpt-4o-mini runs). Top: the gold chain, which passes through two bridge entities the question never names. (a) HippoRAG 2, graph-based method, finds the first bridge entity (Kevin Drew) but no passage about his band or Toronto. (b) LogicRAG, which plans its sub-questions in advance, searches for the city of the performer before finding the performer (dependency error). (c) IRCoT, which keeps all retrieved passages in its long prompt, has the whole chain there and even states that the band is based in Toronto, but then loses track of this fact (tracking error). and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs), until these accumulated QA pairs are enough to answer the original question. Each sub-question names every entity it asks about and does not depend on the answer to any other sub-question. Since nothing is planned in advance, no bridge entity has to be guessed before it is found, and there are no dependencies to get wrong and no sub-question to rewrite. This avoids planning, dependency and rewriting errors, and lets the LLM focus on single fine-grained task at time: writing sub-question for the next missing piece of information. Second, DeFT-RAG converts the remaining LLM work into fine-grained tasks handled outside the LLM. QA table keeps every QA pair and is updated by rules, without any model call, so the LLM no longer has to keep track of what is known, which avoids tracking errors. fine-tuned lightweight decision model (DM), language model trained to answer yes/no questions with probability [22], makes few yes/no decisions: whether question can be answered directly, whether the QA pairs found so far are enough, and whether retrieved passages are relevant, so that the LLM sees more of the needed passages and fewer distracting ones. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when later question asks sub-question with the same meaning, which saves retrieval and LLM calls. Together, these designs raise the accuracy of each step and of the final answer, while making the intermediate answers reusable across questions. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose an incremental question decomposition that generates one self-contained sub-question at time from the original question and the QA pairs found so far. It removes the need to plan sub-questions, decide their dependencies or rewrite them, and lets the LLM focus on single fine-grained task: writing the sub-question for the next missing piece of information. We convert the remaining LLM work into fine-grained tasks handled outside the LLM: rule-based updates to QA table, and yes/no decisions by fine-tuned lightweight DM, such as whether retrieved passages are relevant. This aims to raise the accuracy of each step, and to leave the LLM only few focused, fine-grained tasks that require text generation. We design QA cache that reuses the answers to earlier sub-questions for later questions that ask sub-question with the same meaning, which saves retrieval and LLM calls. We evaluate DeFT-RAG on three multi-hop QA benchmarks with two LLM backbones. It achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method, and reusing answers through the QA cache further reduces LLM calls without lowering accuracy. To support reproducibility, we release our code and prompts at https://github.com/ Dingyi-Kang/DeFT-RAG.

sections.title:
2.2 Multi-Hop Question Answering
A multi-hop question usually cannot be answered from a single
passage [9, 24, 29]. Answering it requires an evidence chain of two
or more facts, each stated in a passage of C, where some facts can
only be found once an earlier one is known. We call the interme-
diate answers that later facts depend on bridge entities: the chain
passes through them, but 𝑄 never names them. For example, to an-
swer “Where do greyhound buses leave from in the city where the
performer of Darlings formed?”, one must first find that Darlings
is an album by Kevin Drew, then that he formed his band, Broken
Social Scene, in Toronto, and only then where Greyhound buses
leave from there (the Toronto Coach Terminal). Kevin Drew and
Toronto are the bridge entities (top of Figure 1).
sections.content: Vanilla RAG (Eq. (1)) handles such questions poorly. Eq. (2) ranks passages only by their similarity to 𝑄, so for the Darlings question it returns passages that share its words, such as passages about greyhound dogs, Greyhound coach model and person named Darling. Answering 𝑄, however, also needs passages about Kevin Drew and Toronto. Because 𝑄 never mentions either of them, their passages rank low, and single retrieval rarely returns the full evidence chain: on MuSiQue, vanilla RAG retrieves it for only 7% of 3-hop questions  (Table 3)  . To address this, two lines of work have been developed: graph-based RAG (2.3) and iterative RAG (2.4).

sections.title:
2.3 Graph-Based RAG
Graph-based RAG methods build a graph over C offline, either by
using an LLM to extract the entities in every passage and the rela-
tions between them [4, 7], or by linking passages across documents
through the entities they share [31]. At answering time, they locate
the entities mentioned in 𝑄 in this graph and follow its links to
collect related passages, instead of ranking passages only by their
similarity to 𝑄 as in Eq. (2). In this way, evidence linked to the ques-
tion’s entities can be retrieved even when it shares little wording
with 𝑄.
sections.content: However, graph-based RAG still falls short in covering the full evidence chain once question needs more than two hops: on MuSiQue, most graph-based methods retrieve the full chain for only 610% of 3-hop questions, barely above vanilla RAG  (Table 3)  ; LinearRAG reaches 28%, but only by giving the LLM about 4,100 words of passages per question, nearly five times as many as vanilla RAG, most of which are not part of the evidence chain. The reason is that most graph-based methods retrieve only once per question, starting from the entities 𝑄 names, while the bridge entities are by definition not mentioned in 𝑄, so the retrieval can reach them only by following graph links from those entities, which rarely gets past the first bridge entity. In Figure 1a, HippoRAG 2 learns from the album passage that Darlings is by Kevin Drew, but retrieves no passage about his band or Toronto, and answers from passage about Greyhound in Philadelphia.

sections.title:
2.4 Iterative RAG
Iterative RAG methods instead aim to find these bridge entities
directly: rather than preprocessing the corpus, they decompose
𝑄 into sub-questions and alternate between retrieval and LLM
reasoning, so that each sub-question can name the bridge entity
found in an earlier step and reach passages that a search with 𝑄
alone would miss. As shown in Table 3, iterative methods retrieve
the full evidence chain for 19–41% of 3-hop questions, well above
most graph-based methods.
sections.content: However, iterative methods often fail, because they ask the LLM to perform several tasks, often within one call: planning subquestions before any of them is answered, deciding the dependency links among them, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. Each of these tasks leads to its own type of error. First, planning errors: methods that plan the sub-questions in advance, such as LogicRAG [3] and REAP [30], must guess bridge entities before finding them, and wrong guess or missing step misleads every later step. For example, asked Who is the owner of the record label of the guitarist who performed on the Top Gun theme?, LogicRAGs plan asks for the label of the themes composer instead of first finding the guitarist, so it answers with the owner of the wrong label. Second, dependency errors: methods that link the sub-questions by their dependencies, such as LogicRAG and REAP, may link them wrongly or in the wrong order, so sub-question is searched before the fact it depends on is found. In Figure 1b, LogicRAG searches for the city where the performer formed before it has found the performer, retrieves passages about bands from other cities, and never searches for the performer at all. Third, rewriting errors: when the answer to sub-question arrives, methods such as Hi-Q [14] and REAP must rewrite the sub-question that depends on it. The LLM may fail to do so, and the sub-question keeps placeholder instead of the entitys name, so retrieval often cannot find the passages about this bridge entity; or it may rewrite the sub-question with the wrong entity. Fourth, tracking errors: methods that carry their whole reasoning history in the prompt, such as IRCoT [25] and Self-Ask [20], must find what is already known within long and growing input, and may miss fact they have already found or ask for it again. In Figure 1c, IRCoTs input holds all three gold passages, and its reasoning states that the band is based in Toronto, yet it then follows passage about Greyhound in Philadelphia and answers with the Philadelphia terminal. Moreover, fixed top-𝑘 retrieval (Eq. (2)), used by most RAG methods, makes these issues worse, because it lowers the answer accuracy of every step. With small 𝑘, part of the needed evidence is missed; with large 𝑘, the evidence is buried among distracting passages. Table 1 illustrates this on MuSiQue questions that can be answered in one retrieval step: widening the list from the top 5 to the top 10 passages raises how often all needed passages are present from 62% to 88%, yet accuracy barely changes (0.620 to 0.630); keeping only the gold passages from the top 10 raises it to 0.793. 2Wiki shows the same pattern. Finally, compared with vanilla RAG and graph-based RAG, iterative methods spend many more retrieval and LLM calls to answer question (Appendix E), which are expensive in latency and cost, yet once question is answered, they discard the intermediate subquestions and answers. This is wasteful: multi-hop questions over the same corpus often share intermediate facts, so these answers could be reused to save retrieval and LLM calls for later questions.

3.1 Incremental Question Decomposition
In DeFT-RAG, the LLM performs only three fine-grained tasks:

LLMsub writes the next sub-question, LLMans answers question from its selected passages, and LLMfin answers the original question from the QA table (blue in Figure 2). LLMsub generates one self-contained sub-question at time from the original question and the QA pairs found so far, asking for the next missing piece of information, until the DM judges these QA pairs enough to answer the original question (3.3). sub-question is self-contained when it names every entity it asks about, by name or by description that needs no other lookup, and does not depend on the answer to any other sub-question, so it can be searched and answered on its own. For example, once the QA table shows that the Rhine ends in the North Sea, Where does the North Sea meet the Atlantic? is self-contained, while Where does that sea meet the Atlantic? is not, because that sea points to an earlier step. Since nothing is planned in advance, no bridge entity has to be guessed before it is found, which avoids the planning errors of 2.4. Since no sub-question depends on another, there are no dependencies to get wrong and no sub-question to rewrite, which avoids dependency and rewriting errors. More importantly, the LLM can focus on single fine-grained task at time: writing sub-question for the next missing piece of information. Together, these improve the quality of the question decomposition and help DeFT-RAG find every bridge entity of the evidence chain: it retrieves the full chain for more questions with three or more hops than any other system in Table 3. sections.title:
3.2 QA Table
DeFT-RAG converts the rest of the work that iterative methods leave
to the LLM into fine-grained tasks handled outside the LLM: rule-
based updates to a QA table, described here, and yes/no decisions
made by the DM (§3.3). This aims to raise the accuracy of each step,
and to leave the LLM only the three tasks in Eq. 3, which require
text generation.
sections.content: Instead of tracking everything found so far within the LLMs context, in long and growing prompt of passages and past reasoning, DeFT-RAG keeps it in compact form, the QA table 𝐹𝑡 of Eq. 3, which starts empty, 𝐹0 = , and grows by one QA pair at each step that finds an answer: 𝐹𝑡 +1 = 𝐹𝑡 {(𝑞𝑡 +1, 𝑎𝑡 +1)}. (4) The QA table is updated by rules, without any LLM or DM call: the QA pair of each answered sub-question is added to the table; subquestion that gets no answer is recorded, and LLMsub is shown it so that it is not asked again; and new sub-question that repeats one already asked is detected by comparing the normalized wording, and LLMsub is asked for another one. Figure 2 shows the QA table for an example question. Every answer found is thus kept explicitly as QA pair, rather than buried in long prompt, which avoids tracking errors. The QA table is the only record of what is known passed from one step to the next: LLMsub reads it to write the next sub-question, the DM reads it to decide whether enough is known to stop, and LLMfin reads it to answer the original question. Since each QA pair is self-contained sub-question with short answer, these inputs stay short and name every entity found so far, instead of carrying long passages or the wording of earlier steps.

3.3 Decision Tasks
The DM is a language model, usually with far fewer parameters
than the backbone LLM, trained to answer yes/no questions with a
probability [22] and fine-tuned for our decisions (§4.2). DeFT-RAG
makes three types of yes/no decisions with it (orange in Figure 2),
which the LLM would otherwise have to make:
sections.content: Relevance: 𝐷rel (𝑞, 𝑝) decides whether retrieved passage 𝑝 is relevant to question 𝑞. Direct answer: 𝐷direct (𝑄, 𝑅𝑤 (𝑄, C)) decides whether the top 𝑤 passages retrieved for the original question, 𝑅𝑤 (𝑄, C), already contain all the evidence needed, so that 𝑄 can be answered in one step. Enough facts: 𝐷suff (𝑄, 𝐹𝑡 ) decides whether the QA pairs found so far are enough to answer 𝑄, which ends the loop. For each decision, the DM reads short input 𝑥, such as question and passage, and returns the probability that the answer is yes. The decision is 𝐷 (𝑥) = (cid:2) 𝑝DM (yes 𝑥) 𝜏 (cid:3), with fixed threshold 𝜏 for each type. Since the DMs probability of yes reflects how often yes is actually right (Appendix C), we use 𝜏 = 0.5, more likely yes than no, for relevance and enough facts, and stricter 𝜏 = 0.7 for direct answer, because question that needs several steps but is wrongly answered directly is unlikely to get the right answer, while question that one step could answer (5) but is wrongly sent to the loop can still get the right answer there, only with more LLM calls. Passage selection. For relevance, the DM keeps, from the top 𝑤 passages retrieved for 𝑞, those relevant to 𝑞: Select(cid:0)𝑞, 𝑅𝑤 (𝑞, C)(cid:1) = { 𝑝 𝑅𝑤 (𝑞, C) : 𝐷rel (𝑞, 𝑝) = 1 }. Because only the selected passages reach the LLM, 𝑤 can be larger than the 𝑘 of the usual top-𝑘 retrieval (Eq. (2)) without burying the evidence among distracting passages (2.4). All settings are listed in Table 6. (6) Fine-tuning. We fine-tune the DM with LoRA [10], using labels derived only from the gold annotations of each benchmarks training split, such as which passages hold the evidence for question and which intermediate answers it needs. No test question is used. Training details are given in Appendix C, and 4.5 shows that finetuning makes the decisions more accurate.

If this does not happen within 𝑇 steps, DeFT-RAG falls back to
answering 𝑄 directly from the relevant passages among the top 2𝑤
retrieved for it (lines 14–15).

sections.title:
4 Evaluation
4.1 Setup
We evaluate on three multi-hop QA benchmarks, MuSiQue [24],
2WikiMultiHopQA (2Wiki) [9] and HotpotQA [29], using the 1,000-
question test set of each and its passage corpus (11,656, 6,119 and
9,811 passages), as released by the authors of LogicRAG [3]. We
compare against 13 baselines: answering without retrieval (No Re-
trieval) and vanilla RAG; seven graph-based methods, LightRAG [6],
PathRAG [2], HippoRAG [7], HippoRAG 2 [8], MemGraphRAG [27],
G3RAG [17] and LinearRAG [31]; and four iterative methods, IR-
CoT [25], Self-Ask [20], LogicRAG [3] and Hi-Q [14]. We do not
compare with REAP [30], whose planner and fact extractor are
LLMs fine-tuned on trajectories from HotpotQA and 2Wiki, which
does not fit our setting of one shared backbone for all systems. All
systems share the same backbone LLM, the same embedding model
(Qwen3-Embedding-4B), temperature 0 and the same output limit;
each baseline otherwise keeps its own published settings, such as
chunk size.
sections.content: We use two backbones: gpt-4o-mini, through its API, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, run locally. All baselines retrieve the top 𝑘 = 5 passages per retrieval. DeFT-RAG retrieves the top 𝑤 = 2𝑘 = 10 passages, from which the DM keeps the relevant ones. For fair comparison, it keeps at most five relevant passages at each step (2.1 to 2.4 on average), the same number as the baselines top-5. DeFT-RAG takes at most 𝑇 = 6 steps, and all main results are obtained without reuse (3.4). We report exact match (EM), token F1 and LLM-judged accuracy (LLM-Acc), our main metric, graded with the SimpleQA prompt [26]. To avoid model grading its own answers, gpt-4o-mini runs are judged by Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.6 runs by gpt-4o-mini. Differences are tested with the exact McNemar test on paired answers. Appendix reports the overhead of every method: index building, answering latency, LLM calls and tokens. Dingyi Kang and Bingzhe Li

sections.content: Graph-based methods vary widely: with gpt-4o-mini, LightRAG, PathRAG and HippoRAG fall below vanilla RAG, and even the strongest of them trail DeFT-RAG by at least 10 points on MuSiQue with either backbone, which matches their low full-chain coverage (2.3). The strongest baselines are iterative methods, but the best of them changes with the benchmark and the backbone: Hi-Q on MuSiQue and HotpotQA, and Self-Ask or LogicRAG on 2Wiki. DeFT-RAG is the only system that is first or on par with the first everywhere.

4.6 Reusing Answers
We run DeFT-RAG with reuse (§3.4) on all 1,000 MuSiQue questions
with gpt-4o-mini, answering them in order with one QA cache.
Of all sub-questions generated over the 1,000 questions, 23.1% are
answered from the cache, which reduces the number of LLM calls by
12.9%. Accuracy does not drop (0.642 with reuse vs. 0.629 without,
𝑝 = 0.18), so answers found for earlier questions can be safely
reused for later ones.
5 Related Work
sections.content: Graph-based RAG. Graph-based methods build graph over the corpus offline and retrieve along it at answering time. GraphRAG [4] and LightRAG [6] extract entities and relations with an LLM and retrieve community summaries or entities, PathRAG [2] retrieves relational paths, HippoRAG [7] and HippoRAG 2 [8] rank passages with Personalized PageRank from the questions entities, MemGraphRAG [27] builds layered graph of schemas, facts and passages, and LinearRAG [31] and G3RAG [17] build their graphs without LLM extraction. All of these methods retrieve once per question, starting from what the question names, which rarely recovers the full evidence chain beyond two hops (2.3). DeFT-RAG instead finds the bridge entities at answering time, one self-contained subquestion at time, and retrieves the full chain for more questions with three or more hops than any of these methods  (Table 3)  . Iterative RAG. IRCoT [25] uses each new chain-of-thought sentence as the next query, and Self-Ask [20] poses follow-up questions within single growing prompt. LogicRAG [3] and REAP [30] plan the sub-questions with their dependencies in advance, and Hi-Q [14] and REAP rewrite dependent sub-questions as answers arrive. In these methods, the LLM itself takes on several tasks, often within the same call: planning or writing the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them, keeping track of what is known, and deciding when to stop. DeFT-RAG instead lets the LLM focus on single fine-grained task at time: generating one selfcontained sub-question for the next missing piece of information, which removes planning, dependencies and rewriting, and avoids their associated errors; tracking is handled by the QA table, and the yes/no decisions by the fine-tuned DM. Its LLM input stays short, 1,569 tokens per question against 6,140 for Self-Ask (Appendix E), and it achieves the highest accuracy of these methods in every setting  (Table 2)  . Models for retrieval decisions. Rerankers [18, 23] re-score retrieved passages but still keep fixed number, and AdaptiveRAG [12] uses trained classifier to choose between no, single and iterative retrieval; Self-RAG [1], Search-R1 [13], R1-Searcher [21] and Search-o1 [16] instead train the backbone LLM, or use reasoning model, to make such decisions. DeFT-RAG uses one fine-tuned DM for the yes/no decisions at every step while the backbone stays unchanged, so any LLM can serve as the backbone, and fine-tuning the DM is much cheaper than training the backbone LLM.

sections.title:
6 Conclusion
We presented DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework for multi-hop ques-
tion answering built on three components: incremental decompo-
sition into self-contained sub-questions, which avoids planning,
dependency and rewriting errors; fine-grained tasks handled out-
side the LLM, namely rule-based updates to a QA table and yes/no
decisions by a fine-tuned lightweight DM; and a QA cache that
reuses answers across questions. Across three benchmarks and
two backbones, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thir-
teen baselines, with its largest gains on MuSiQue, while giving the
LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method; reusing
answers reduces LLM calls without lowering accuracy.

No: They differ in entity, property, time, place or scope -- OR either one refers to something without naming it (such as "the tournament" or "the author"), so it is unclear whether they mean the same thing. Decision Model Fine-Tuning Details Training questions and corpora. For each benchmark, we sample 3,000 questions from its training split, following the mix of hop counts or question types of the test set, and split them into groups of 1,000. Each groups corpus consists of the passages of its own questions (MuSiQue about 13,000, 2Wiki about 5,200, HotpotQA about 9,600 passages per group, close to the test corpora of 11,656, 6,119 and 9,811). Every training request retrieves its top 10 passages from its groups corpus with the embedder and query instruction of DeFT-RAG. Labels. All labels come from the training splits gold annotations. Relevance: passage is relevant if it is gold supporting passage; each request labels all gold passages and three randomly chosen other passages, while all ten passages stay in the request. Direct answer: yes if all gold supporting passages are among the top 10. Enough facts: built from the gold decompositions (MuSiQue) and gold evidence (2Wiki): the answers to only the first steps give no, the answers to all steps give yes, wrong answer to step gives no, and the answers to all steps plus an unrelated QA pair give yes. We add enough-facts items taken from runs of DeFT-RAG on training questions, labelled by the same rule, and items whose QA pairs use self-contained sub-questions, as DeFT-RAG writes them. The same-meaning decision is not fine-tuned. DeFT-RAG: Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers Leakage checks. All 1,000 test questions of each benchmark come from its official validation split; none of them is in the training data, and no training question text is identical to test question. Training questions whose gold passage appears in any test corpus are skipped, so that no test-corpus passage is ever shown in training. Training and probability adjustment. The final data has 48,036 training and 7,806 development examples. LoRA settings are given in 4.2; training used micro-batches of 8,192 tokens, gradient accumulation to an effective batch equal to the base models single-GPU default, gradient checkpointing and gradient clipping at 1.0. single temperature for yes/no probabilities is fitted on the development examples (1.08). Experimental Details for Baselines All systems use the same backbone, the same embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-4B, last-token pooling, with the query instruction applied to queries only), temperature 0, top-𝑝 = 1 and the same output limit of 3,072 tokens; the reasoning mode of Qwen3.6 is turned off for every system. Each baseline keeps the settings of its released code or paper that define the method, such as chunk size and graph construction, and all baselines retrieve the top 𝑘 = 5 passages per retrieval (4.1). Systems that build the same kind of index share it: HippoRAG and MemGraphRAG reuse the index built by HippoRAG 2 (for MemGraphRAG, only the passage embeddings, after we checked that the passage sets are identical), and PathRAG reuses LightRAGs graph. Every systems answers are graded by the same script with the same judge prompt, and missing answers count as wrong. Overhead Analysis Table 7 reports, for every method with gpt-4o-mini, the cost of building the index and the cost of answering each question. Its last row replaces the local DM of DeFT-RAG with Jev, closed decision model accessed through an API. Index. DeFT-RAG, vanilla RAG and the iterative methods only embed the passages, which takes about five minutes per corpus and no LLM calls. The graph-based methods that extract graph with the LLM need from about 2,100 (LightRAG) to 147,000 (MemGraphRAG) LLM calls and 11 to 114 million tokens per corpus, and up to 18 hours of build time; this cost is paid again when the corpus changes. Answering. DeFT-RAG gives the LLM fewer input tokens per question than every other iterative method (1,569, against 1,926 to 13,928), and it produces the fewest output tokens of all methods (33), because each task asks for short output; it also makes fewer LLM calls than Self-Ask and Hi-Q (4.8, against 6.3 and 6.6). Its latency is the highest (median 9.9 s). Where the latency comes from. Most of the answering time of DeFT-RAG goes to its frequent calls to the local DM, which selects the relevant passages at every step and makes the other decisions. Per question, DeFT-RAG makes 7.0, 6.3 and 3.2 DM calls on MuSiQue, 2Wiki and HotpotQA, at 1.6 to 1.8 each, as the DM runs on one GPU, one request at time, over inputs of up to ten passages. These calls take 12.5 of the 20.4 mean answering time on MuSiQue, 10.3 of 16.7 on 2Wiki and 5.2 of 7.8 on HotpotQA, about 60 to 70%. With Jev in place of the DM, at about 0.16 per call, the median latency falls from 9.9 to 5.0 s, and the mean answering time to 8.2, 7.7 and 3.6 on the three benchmarks, while accuracy stays within 1.2 points of the DMs (0.618, 0.857 and 0.867, against 0.629, 0.852 and 0.874). Most of the added latency thus comes from how the DM is served, not from the method itself.
